newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Efforts to close Hebron deal by Christmas.
newsitem.headline: Efforts to close Hebron deal by Christmas.

text.p: The PLO and Israel with the aid of Washington and Cairo are pushing to clinch a deal on the long-delayed Israeli handover of the West Bank town of Hebron by Christmas, PLO officials said on Sunday.
"We are studying documents which include proposals to close a deal on Hebron," chief PLO negtiator Mahmoud Abbas, better known as Abu Mazen, told Reuters.
"If things move ahead, we expect a deal before Christmas," Abbas told Reuters. "But right now, I can't say if we have made progress or not".

Officials said proposals to close a deal on Hebron were summarised last week in a document drafted by Israeli and Palestinian negotiators with the aid of U.S. Middle East peace coordinator Dennis Ross and Egyptian official Osama al-Baz.
One PLO official said: "The PLO leadership and the Palestinian cabinet discussed a three-page document. Some ideas were approved and others were rejected, so alternative amendments were proposed."

He said Palestinian President Yasser Arafat discussed the document with Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo on Saturday, and left behind PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat to draft amendments together with Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa.
"After the sides have narrowed the gaps and after agreeing on the main disputed issues, President Arafat will meet Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu," the official said.
Israeli government spokesman Moshe Fogel said: "There have been constant discussions on possible frameworks for an agreement, and constant contacts on the wording and phrasing".
PLO officials said proposals in the document would mean concessions by both sides.
Palestinians would concede that their 400 policemen who will be deployed in Hebron would carry pistols and not rifles in areas close to Jewish enclaves in Hebron.
They said Israel would retract its demand its army have the right to re-enter areas under PLO control.

The points have long snagged the two-month negotiations on implementing the Hebron deal, which was signed more than a year ago by Israel's previous government and the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO).
Getting the points accepted will be a rocky process.

PLO officials said on Sunday that Israel had agreed to gradually reopen al-Shuhada (Martyrs) street in the heart of Hebron over a four-month period so that life could return to normal in Hebron's Old City.

Al-Shuhada street was closed to Palestinian traffic in February 1994 after a Jewish settler massacred 29 Palestinian worshippers in al-Ibrahimi mosque, also known as the Tomb of the Patriarchs, revered by Moslems and Jews.
Most of the fortified enclaves in which the 400 Jews of Hebron have settled amidst its 100,000 Palestinians are along al-Shuhada street.
Witnesses said Israeli bulldozers removed the cement blockades at entrances to the street, but Palestinian traffic was still barred. Opening the street has been one of the key Palestinian demands.
